k-1.x_notes: Seven substantial problems at actual size, mathematically correct and well sequenced. The hexagon's pieces by color, then all the ways to fill it with 'same pieces = same way' (10 multisets, 12 hexagons provided). Counting greens in triangles of side 2-4 with a side-5 prediction. Fewest greens with blues on the same triangles (2, 3, 4, predict 5). Six blue-only yes/no shapes, including an even-area impossible one, with 'how do you know?'. Fewest pieces for the side-3 triangle (3 trapezoids beats hexagon + 3 greens) and the big hexagon. An inventive finale: build 6- and 8-triangle shapes blue cannot fill. Real kernel-1 thinking that never feels dumbed down, with enough for 40 minutes. Weaknesses: a Name field on every page and a header without week/activity; the footer is only a page number. The side-5 prediction questions are abstract for kindergartners, and P3 leans toward counting practice.
k-1.y_notes: Clean format that meets the standard: Week/Tiling/K-1 header, footer, one shared rule, picture legends that help non-readers. All answers check out. P1: cover and color hexagons with green/blue/red (7 combinations, 9 boards). P2: fewest blocks on a side-3 triangle, a 2x2 rhombus and a side-2 hexagon. P3: blue-only yes/no on five shapes, including an even-area impossible trapezoid and a tileable star. P4: fewest greens on triangles of side 2-4. P5: all rhombus tilings of the unit hexagon (2) and the 2-1-1 hexagon (3), a gentle kernel-2 entry. Weaknesses: only five problems, mostly do-and-record or circle yes/no, with no 'how do you know', no prediction, and no inventing. It is closer to the 'too few, ends early' K-1 the organizer complains about, and the coloring is partly busywork.
k-1.reason: X gives K-1 more and deeper concrete work (an explanation prompt, pattern prediction, and inventing impossible shapes) while staying hands-on at actual size. Y is clean but thinner and more closed. X's Name field and header are quick fixes.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Excellent, correct kernel-1 development; I verified every board. P1: five boards, including a balanced tileable odd shape (D), even-area imbalanced boards (B, C) and an odd-area board (E). P2: hexagon with an up and a down hole (tileable) vs two down holes (not). P3: children choose two holes on a side-2 hexagon; all 144 up/down pairs work and same-orientation pairs never do, a Gomory-style discovery. P4: a color-balanced board J that still cannot be tiled, showing that counting is necessary but not sufficient. P5: fewest greens on triangles of side 3-6 at actual size. P6: sides 10 and 100 with 'how do you know'. P7: chevron packings (side 4 leaves 4, side 5 leaves 5) and whether purple ever beats blue. P8: boards purple covers but blue doesn't, and vice versa. Plenty for 40 minutes. Weaknesses: a Name field on every page, a nonstandard header and a page-number-only footer; 8 pages, some holding a single board.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Tight, correct and well formatted, with header/footer, shared rules, legends and recording lines. P1: four yes/no boards (2 yes, 2 even-area no), with drawing. P2: fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5 with drawn coverings. P3: re-cover with chevrons ('can chevrons help? explain'). P4: a 2-2-1 hexagon with two black holes on four boards (J and M no, K and L yes; verified). P5: prove the 4-green bound and generalize to side 10. P6: an excellent open design problem, a 16-triangle board needing the most greens (max 6). Weaknesses: no balanced-but-impossible example, so children may conclude counting is the whole story. Holes are given rather than chosen. Several write-an-explanation tasks for third graders.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are strong and correct. X's development is richer: free hole choice leading to a clean theorem, a balanced board that still fails, and concrete chevron packings. Y is tidier, and its design problem is excellent.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Rich, correct kernel-2 sequence; I checked the counts and flip distances. P1: tilings of a 1-2-2 hexagon (6). P2: drawing the flip map (a 2x2 Young lattice) and its farthest pair. P3: ribbons with a worked RLRR example; for a=1 boards the ribbon determines the tiling. P4: counts of 10 and 70 via ribbons. P5: the 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon. P6: build X and flip to Y (4 flips). P7: diameter (8). P8: odd round trips. P9: the cube-stack interpretation and a box of 8. Boards are at actual size, with copies for drawing. Weaknesses: a Name field and nonstandard header/footer; the ribbon paragraph is wordy. The ribbon only counts single-ribbon boards and is never used to prove flip facts. The parity question (P8) comes before the cube picture (P9) that answers it, and 9 problems is more than the hour holds.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Very well developed and correct; distances and chain pairs verified. P1: an accessible entry family (2, 3, 4 tilings) generalized to top edge 10, giving 11 with explanation. P2: a 2-2-1 hexagon (6 tilings) with 'how do you know you have them all'. P3: concrete flips from S to T (8), S to U (3) and U to T (5) on an actual-size board, with a flip picture. P4: two R/L chains defined with a picture, plus four chain-pair puzzles (two exist, two impossible because the chains would cross). P5: the 20 tilings. P6: discover that a move swaps an adjacent RL pair. P7: prove the 8-move lower bound and that round trips are even. This follows the outline's use of ribbons to prove flip facts closely, and the format matches the standard. Weaknesses: no cube-stack connection, and large lined areas for written explanations.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are excellent and correct. Y's sequence has a gentler entry and uses the chains to explain flips and parity, as the outline intends, and its pages need no format fixes. X's flip map and cube view are nice extras, but its parity question comes before the tool that answers it.

overall.reason: X is clearly better for K-1, slightly better for grades 2-3 and slightly behind for 4-5. Its mathematics is correct and deep throughout, at actual size, with enough work for each band. Y follows the organizer's page format better, but X's format faults (Name field, header and footer) can be fixed within the fifteen minutes per band, while Y's thinner K-1 set would need new problems written.
